question: MCI against healthy older adults (P-83: 15 participants aged 63-83 in Magdeburg, aMCI and naMCI; P-214: community screening cohorts in Shanghai). The population class matches, and the shared channel is EEG: P-83 adds heart-rate variability recorded during CERAD sub-tests, and P-214 adds eye tracking, a 20-subtest neuropsychological battery and demographics to one-electrode EEG. Cohort, features, architecture, sample size and validation design differ, which the rule allows.
metric: Accuracy with accuracy (same type). The unit differs: P-83 scores 3-second signal windows, with windows of the same 15 people shuffled across its 75/25 split, while P-214 scores subjects in 5-fold CV and on an independent cohort. As in C-117, subjects are taken as n for the uncertainty.

figures.P-83: Hybrid SVM/GB/RF voting on EEG+HRV windows: average accuracy over seven CERAD tests 93.86% (sensitivity 93.87%, specificity 93.53%); best test T1 97.43% (10-fold 95.23%, LOOCV 96.14%). Evaluation unit = windows of 15 subjects, so no subject-level test count is reported. Wilson with n = 15 subjects: 93.86% [0.709, 0.990]; T1 97.43% [0.757, 0.998]. P-214's pipeline re-implemented on P-83's data (Table 9): average 87.68%, Wilson n = 15 [0.633, 0.967].
figures.P-214: RBF SVM on MRMR-selected EEG, eye-tracking, neuropsychological and demographic features: Cohort 1, 5-fold CV on 336 subjects, 84.5 +/- 4.43% (AUC 0.942), Wilson [0.802, 0.880]; Cohort 2, independent test on 92 subjects (44 MCI/48 NC) from another district, 88.8 +/- 3.59% (AUC 0.966), Wilson [0.807, 0.938].

matched_figure_check: A matched figure exists and reconciles the pair. P-83 ran P-214's method on its own data (Table 9): the average accuracy is 87.68%, which lies inside both of P-214's intervals ([0.802, 0.880] and [0.807, 0.938]), and P-214's 84.5% and 88.8% lie inside the interval of the re-implementation. With the method held to P-214's, P-83's data reproduce P-214's accuracy. The remaining gap (93.86% against 87.68%) is P-83's own method comparison on its own 15-subject, window-level data, which that paper shows directly. On subject-level uncertainty the headline gap also runs one way only. 93.86% lies outside P-214's CV interval and, by 0.001, outside its independent-cohort interval. But 84.5% and 88.8% lie well inside P-83's interval [0.709, 0.990].
performance_validity: P-83 meets the Section 3.5 exclusion in substance, as recorded in C-74: its best result is 97.43% accuracy (LOOCV 96.14%) on internal validation of 15 subjects with windows of the same people shuffled across training and test, and no external cohort. The compared 93.86% is the cross-test average of that same evaluation. Section 3.5 names segment-level splitting as a design that inflates accuracy. P-214 (84.5%, 88.8%; AUC 0.942, 0.966, with an independent cohort) is not excluded.

candidate_explanations.difference: Evaluation unit and split (window-level shuffling within 15 people vs subject-level CV and an independent cohort). Not needed to explain the gap, because the matched re-implementation already reconciles it.
candidate_explanations.quote: For each test, we separated our data into 75% for the training set and 25% for the testing set. To boost the effectiveness of ML model accuracy and to reduce the rate of overfitting, we applied the shuffling strategy throughout the data partitioning process.

reason: P-83 reports P-214's method on its own data (87.68%), and this agrees with P-214's own accuracies (84.5% and 88.8%) within uncertainty, so the papers' data dissolve the gap (condition 3). What remains is P-83's in-paper method comparison on 15 subjects. P-83 also meets the near-ceiling small-sample exclusion (97.43% on window-level internal validation of 15 people), so a performance comparison resting on it fails condition 5. With subjects as n, the headline gap is beyond uncertainty in one direction only.
